title: The heartwood
hook: a man seeking heartwood who settles for twigs, bark or sapwood

segments.voice: Yesterday: hatthipada, and your line, not yet the elephant. Did you wait for more tracks before deciding about someone? Day four hundred twenty-six.

Build a fire with green branches and you meet the problem fast. It smokes, it hisses, it goes out. The good wood is inside: the dense, dark center of an old tree that burns slow and lasts. Carpenters want it too. It doesn't rot, it doesn't warp. You can't get to it without cutting through everything else first: the leaves, the bark, the pale sapwood. And it's tempting to stop halfway. Today: the heartwood.
screen: `GREEN BRANCHES SMOKE AND GO OUT.` → `THE GOOD WOOD IS AT THE CENTER.` → `TEMPTING TO STOP HALFWAY.`

segments.voice: This is the twenty-ninth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. It was given, the text says, not long after Devadatta, the Buddha's cousin, had split away from the community. The Buddha describes a man who needs heartwood. He goes into the forest, finds a great tree, and walks past the heartwood, past the sapwood, past the inner bark and the outer bark, and cuts off twigs and leaves. He carries them home thinking he's got heartwood. A man with good eyes would say: he doesn't know what heartwood is. His work won't get done. Then the Buddha maps the tree. Someone goes forth out of faith, and gains gifts, honor and fame. Pleased with that, they look down on others. That's the twigs and leaves. Someone else doesn't stop there and becomes truly virtuous, but stops pleased with their virtue. That's the outer bark. Another goes on to deep concentration, and stops there. Inner bark. Another reaches knowledge and vision, and stops. Sapwood. And then the discourse says the goal plainly. This holy life is not for gifts and fame, not for virtue alone, not for concentration alone, not for knowledge and vision alone. It's for the unshakable freedom of mind. That is the heartwood. Notice: none of the outer layers is bad. Virtue is good. Concentration is good. They're part of the same tree. The mistake is only in stopping, pleased with yourself, and calling bark heartwood. It's an easy mistake in any serious work. The applause, the good habits, the skills: real, and still not the center.
screen: `TWIGS AND LEAVES: GIFTS AND FAME` · `BARK: VIRTUE, THEN CONCENTRATION` · `SAPWOOD: KNOWLEDGE AND VISION` · `HEARTWOOD: UNSHAKABLE FREEDOM OF MIND` · then, large: `TAKE THE HEARTWOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go for the heartwood. Pick one thing you care about: your work, your practice, a relationship. Sit, and ask what its twigs and leaves are: the praise, the likes, the look of it. Then what its bark is: the good habits around it. Then ask quietly what's at the center, the part that would still matter if nobody saw. Rest your attention there for the rest of the sit, as if your hand were on the grain of the wood. The bell holds the time.
The heartwood. Sara in Pali: the dense core of the tree, past the leaves, the bark and the sapwood. The unshakable freedom the path is for. Today's word.
Your line: take the heartwood. Today, when praise or a small success comes, enjoy it, and then ask what's still at the center. Day four hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the heartwood simile to remind monastics and lay practitioners that reputation, good conduct, concentration and insight are stages of the path, and that liberation of mind is its goal.

match.prompt: map the tree — tap the pairs.

myth: the Buddha says virtue and concentration are worthless
they're real layers of the same tree; the mistake is stopping there, pleased, and calling bark heartwood.
the text places this talk soon after Devadatta split away
MN 29 opens not long after Devadatta left the community.
the man in the story carries home sapwood
the first man walks past everything else and carries home twigs and leaves, thinking it's heartwood.

fork.setup: you went forth, and people now bring you gifts and praise your name. what does the Buddha's simile call that?
fork.reveal: gifts, honor and fame are the twigs and leaves: the outermost part of the tree, the furthest from the heartwood.

original.note: Pali sara: heartwood, the core or essence. the discourse is the Mahasaropama Sutta, the greater simile of the heartwood.

trapdoor: what you thought: be a good person and you've arrived.
what it means: goodness, focus and insight are layers of the tree; the path is for unshakable freedom at its center.
what a scholar hears: Pali sara means both heartwood and essence, so the simile's title carries both senses at once.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 29, Mahasaropama Sutta (the greater simile of the heartwood)

notes: MN 29 paraphrased. Order of layers (twigs and leaves, outer bark, inner bark, sapwood, heartwood) matched to gain/honor, virtue, concentration, knowledge and vision, unshakable liberation: confirm.
